newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian industry revival unlikely soon - economists.
newsitem.headline: Indian industry revival unlikely soon - economists.

text.p: A revival in India's slackening industrial growth in the financial year's fourth quarter is unlikely to materialise, economists warned on Friday, saying government projections were too optimistic.
"The improvement is unlikely to come in 1996/97," said R. Venkatesan, industry division head at the National Council for Applied Economic Research (NCAER), a Delhi-based think-tank.
In its February report on the Indian economy, securities firm ING Barings cautioned about the "illusion of growth" in the last quarter.
"Everyone acknowledged the existence of a slowdown in industrial production during the first to third quarters of 1996/97 and predicted a revival thereafter," ING Barings said.
"However, it would seem that people are wishing that the worst is over; there is very little cogent evidence to prove the revival theory."
Officials have said overall growth measured by the index of industrial production (IIP) will see an improvement in the last quarter of the 1996/97 fiscal year ending March 31.
They said the lagged effect of an easier monetary policy and the strength of the agricultural sector will boost growth.
The latest available data showed that IIP increased by 9.8 percent during April-October 1996, down from 11.7 percent in the same period a year ago.
"The last quarter growth will be encouraging," Industry Minister Murasoli Maran told Reuters on Thursday, forecasting double-digit growth for the year.
But economists pitched 1996/97 industrial growth at a modest 6 percent to 8 percent.
"The government is being too optimistic," said economist Rajan Govil at securities firm James Capel B&K.
Analysts said strong agricultural growth coupled with increased food grain prices would result in rising rural incomes, spurring demand for consumer goods.
But the impact on the industrial sector is likely to be later than officials expect, they said.
Govil -- who pegs annual industrial growth at 7.8 percent -- said the slowdown was unlikely to be arrested until March, when an upswing in rural incomes would drive demand higher.
"The first quarter of the next financial year should see some improvement as agricultural growth results in increased rural spending," NCAER's Venkatesan said.
Sectors most likely to benefit initially are auto, personal care, consumer durables, cement, paints, textiles and tobacco, the economists said.
Agricultural growth, spurred by plentiful monsoon rains, has been forecast to grow by around 3.7 percent in the current financial year, after contracting 0.1 percent in 1995/96.
Analysts said a recovery in industrial growth would also depend on what incentives the government offered Indian industry in the federal budget, due on February 28.
